implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's exceptions and adds one structural problem: `strictNullChecks` gives it the machinery to express a missing result, and that machinery is frequently unused in favour of `throw new Error('not found')`. The remedy is usually the simplest of the ones in this catalogue — return `T | undefined` and check it at the call site — with a discriminated union where the failure carries data, and `never` in the return type to make the compiler verify that every throw path is handled. The same discipline as everywhere applies: do not throw on a path that runs on every request.
idiom_name: thrown Error as a result; the absent language-level Result type
pitfalls: `throw new Error('...')` with no code loses the machine-readable part that made the error matchable.
A `catch (e)` without checking `e instanceof Error` means a thrown string is typed as an Error by TypeScript and fails at runtime.
`never` return types on exhaustive switches are what make the compiler catch a new error variant; removing them removes the check.
Rejecting a promise to signal a 'no result' turns every call site into a try/catch instead of a check.
